goal/add: With learned positions, each slot has its own vector, a row of P, added to the embedding of the token sitting there.
goal/back: But much of what a query looks for is relative, like the word just before it: the key at four, for a query at five, or the key at eight, for a query at nine.
goal/twice: To added vectors, those two cases share nothing. Rows five and four of P are one pair, rows nine and eight another, so the model has to learn the word before afresh at every slot.
goal/want: Better if the score depended only on how far apart the query and the key sit: the gap, which is one in both cases.
goal/su: In 2021, Jianlin Su and colleagues found a way. Instead of adding a vector, turn each query and each key by an angle set by its position.
goal/name: They called it rotary position embedding, rope for short. Rotary, because it rotates. Position embedding, after vectors like P, though here nothing is added.
turn/pair: Start with one pair of a query: two and one, the arrow q from rotation. Here is that same pair at positions zero to four, one dial each.
turn/theta: Each step of position turns it a fixed angle further, written theta, the Greek letter theta. Here, thirty degrees.
turn/m: Write m for the position. At position m, the pair has turned by m times theta.
turn/three: So position zero does not turn at all, and position three turns three times thirty degrees: ninety degrees.
turn/wrap: But one pair alone soon comes round. Twelve steps of thirty degrees make a full turn, so position twelve looks just like position zero.
turn/pairs: So the d k entries of a query are cut into d k over two pairs, and each pair turns at its own speed. Here, pair one turns only three degrees a step.
turn/clock: It works like the hands of a clock. The fast hand tells neighbors apart, and a slow one still tells twelve from zero, long after the fast hand has come round.
turn/speeds: With d k of sixty four, the paper's thirty two pairs run from about fifty seven degrees a step, the fastest, to under a hundredth of a degree, the slowest.
turn/only: Nothing is learned, and nothing is added to the token. Just before scoring, every query and every key is turned by its own position.
relative/both: Why does turning help? Turn a query and a key by the same angle, and they move together: the angle between them stays, and so does their dot product.
relative/numbers: Two, one dotted with one, one is three. Turned ninety degrees each, they still give three.
relative/apart: Now put a query at position five, turned by five theta, and a key at position two, turned by two theta. They end up three theta apart: one theta for each step between them.
relative/shift: Move both four places later, to nine and six. Each turns four theta more, together, so the angle between them stays, and so does the score.
relative/distance: So the score depends only on how far apart the two sit, and which comes first. The word before now looks the same at every slot, and is learned once.
relative/try: Try one, with theta of ninety degrees: the query two, one at position one, and the key one, one at position zero.
relative/tq: The query makes one quarter turn, which swaps its entries and flips the new first sign: minus one, two. The key, at position zero, does not turn.
relative/tdot: Dot them: minus one, plus two. The score is one, where the unturned pair gave three.
